name: Rafael Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play accordion backing for a local dance troupe, record simple melody demos and help one beginner under the bandleader. I finished secondary school and turned to paid music after years driving deliveries; at 58 I still need the lead player to check a quick change. I like seeing people stand up when the first tune starts.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of the work affects home life?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner cooks at a community clinic on regular shifts, and our children are grown. We rent a flat and have three months of expenses saved. My music income is typical for this junior role, with some similar groups nearby, though I cannot live on a job posting that is not open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the troupe that faster date lists help if the written fee stays with every dance. A machine does not notice when the dancers need a slower tune.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three months saved and my partner’s clinic wage cover an occasional late demo payment. I still want a signed season, but I do not expect this mild AI change to remove the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid dance sets, one assisted beginner and simple demos this season. I use AI daily to make practice and booking lists, then check each tune with the lead player and the paper score; before next season I would ask for a written cancellation fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about current bills. We could handle one delayed fee without calling our grown children for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a dance date move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A hall leak moved a Saturday show last spring. I received the rehearsal fee but not the show fee, so I would ask for a half-fee clause.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why check the tune with the leader?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lead player catches the chord I rush. A full room can hear one wrong bass note better than I can.

I would say **machines miss dancers’ tempo** when a tune needs slowing.
think: Our **three-month reserve** and partner wage absorb one late demo fee.
The **dance season** still needs signed terms, even with mild AI.
do: Keep **paid dance sets**, assisted beginner and demos this season.
Request a **written half-fee clause** before next season.
feel: I feel **calm** while current paid work and household wages hold.

fieldNote: His **late-entry junior skill** fits simple accordion parts and assisted beginner teaching.
Daily **AI lists** are existing use, checked against paper music and the lead player.

steps.text: Keep paid dance-troupe sets, assisted beginner and demos this season
Request written half-fee cancellation clause before next season

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the dance manager that generated melody demos could replace small recording orders. I would ask for the live dates and paid revision fees in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Demos provide about a quarter of my own musician pay. If clients buy fewer, our three-month reserve gives us time to search, but not a new monthly wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would ask the manager for three months of paid dates and a paid sound-engineer lesson on a new AI audio cleaner, which removes background hiss from a recorded accordion line. In the first year I would test it only on my own nameless demo with the troupe’s licence and approved local storage, compare the cleaned line with the original by ear, and stop if a note changes or the file leaves the troupe’s system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about demo income shrinking. I can learn a new tool early. Someone must still buy my accordion demo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put a beginner’s recording into the cleaner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would use a take I own. A learner’s sound and name stay out unless there is written consent and a clear storage rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a subscription?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the troupe must cover the licence and training hour. I would return to my original recording if a trial cost me money.

I would warn that **generated demos** could remove recording work.
think: My **melody demos** provide about a quarter of my pay.

Test **audio cleaner** after paid engineer lesson on owned nameless demo with troupe licence/local storage; compare by ear, stop errors/leakage.
feel: I feel **anxious** about realistic cuts to my own demo pay.
S1.quote: Someone must still buy my accordion demo.
fieldNote: His **new tool learning** needs paid instruction, troupe licence, owned nameless music and manual comparison.
Approved **local storage** and a note/privacy stop prevent unsafe demo use.

steps.text: Test audio cleaner after paid engineer lesson on own nameless demo, troupe licence/storage; listen, stop errors/leakage
Keep paid dance/beginner calls while requesting three months of written paid dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the troupe that thinking AGI by 2028 could make simple melody demos quickly. Accordion-playing robots follow around 2031, three years later, so the paid recording could end first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect demo orders to stop in 2028, removing a quarter of my pay. Some dance sets might also be cut, but there are local venues to ask if that happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would total demo invoices and ask for a signed paid dance calendar. In the first year after 2028, if paid dance dates fall too, I would seek a posted arts-centre room technician job only if my secondary schooling and delivery experience meet its requirements, written net pay after travel beats lost music fees and the bus route works; I would keep current sets and the beginner until a written offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the expected demo loss, with three months saved and some local options. I would be alarmed if dance work collapsed too, but I cannot say it will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at 60 instead of applying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would first get an actual pension statement. Three months saved does not tell me how to pay years of rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the room job open?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would apply only to a posted paid opening with written hours. I cannot leave the troupe for an old advert.

I would warn **demo pay** could end before accordion-playing robots arrive.
think: I expect **demo orders** to end in 2028, removing a quarter of my own music pay.
Paid **dance cuts** remain possible, not certain, while current sets still have bookings.
do: Count **demo invoices** and request signed paid dates now.
Seek **posted room work** after 2028 dance cuts if secondary schooling/delivery experience qualify, after-travel net beats losses and buses fit.
Keep **sets and beginner** until signed offer; obtain actual pension statement before deciding to stop.

fieldNote: The likely **2028 demo loss** precedes 2031 accordion-playing robots.
A room job needs **posted eligibility**, written net replacement pay, reachable bus hours and signed offer.

Obtain actual pension statement before stopping paid work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the troupe that five years until AGI by 2031 gives me time to learn paid sound work. Playing robots follow around 2034, after demo-making changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Demos could end by 2031. A funded room-sound course might lead to paid work, but a certificate alone does not pay rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This autumn I would seek an actual paid six-month room-sound training place only if the arts centre funds tuition and the study shifts do not replace paid dance dates without equal wages. In the first year after 2031, if demos end and paid sets fall, I would apply for a posted venue sound-assistant job only if the certificate qualifies me, written net pay after travel beats lost music fees and the buses run at shift end; I would keep troupe work and the beginner until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious until the training and the job are paid. Five years of warning is useful only if I can keep earning while learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you wire a speaker alone after training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the venue sound lead must supervise my first checks. I would not handle live wiring until the safety checklist is signed and the lead approves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if tuition is covered but study hours are unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid dance dates and ask about another intake. Free room-sound tuition is not an income plan.

Keep **troupe and beginner** until signed offer; work under sound lead until live-wiring sign-off.

fieldNote: The **training gate** includes actual paid place, funded tuition and no lost weekly wages.
The new job needs **posted qualification**, written net replacement pay, reachable buses and supervised wiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that ten years until AGI by 2036 is time to check what retirement actually pays. Accordion-playing robots follow around 2039, but a new date does not make rent go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may still need dance and lesson fees. Three months saved gives us room to plan, but I cannot assume any pension payment without a statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would request a real pension statement and save twenty percent of each extra paid dance set after rent, food and bus fares until our reserve reaches six months. In the first year after 2036 I would keep paid sets and the beginner while booked and, if dance fees fall, seek a posted arts-centre room attendant job only if my secondary schooling and delivery experience meet its requirements, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the bus times work; I would leave current work only after a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel uneasy about distant work, with current sets paid and three months saved. I would keep earning at 68 if the pension and paid jobs did not cover rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no extra set pays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I put nothing into savings from that source. I would not move food money to make the account look stronger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a job title be enough to leave music?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would need posted paid hours and a written net wage after travel. A room-attendant title without adequate wages will not pay the flat rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because demo pay could end before another paid job opens. Signed dance dates, an actual pension statement and a posted qualifying sound role with written net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a late beginner can learn sound work and keep earning. I practise the slow accordion line after supper, but rent still needs a paid Saturday.

headlineQuote: I practise the slow accordion line after supper, but rent still needs a paid Saturday.
portrait: At **58**, Rafael is a junior accordionist with secondary schooling, a partner, grown children and three months saved.
His **typical musician pay** comes from dance sets, simple demos and one assisted beginner, with some local jobs.
He uses **AI daily** for lists and learns new audio cleanup only after paid engineer instruction on his own take.
He considers **paid sound training** and a posted job, while checking actual pension income before slowing down.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end demo fees before another paid role is real.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed dance dates**, an actual pension statement and a qualifying posted sound job with written net pay would help Rafael.
